description_full: H.B. Fuller Company, together with its subsidiaries, formulates, manufactures, and markets adhesives, sealants, coatings, polymers, tapes, encapsulants, additives, and other specialty chemical products. It operates through three segments: Hygiene, Health and Consumable Adhesives; Engineering Adhesives; and Building Adhesive Solutions. The Hygiene, Health and Consumable Adhesives segment produces and supplies specialty industrial adhesives, such as thermoplastic, thermoset, reactive, water-based, and solvent-based products for applications in various markets, including packaging, converting, nonwoven and hygiene, and medical and beauty. The Engineering Adhesives segment produces and supplies high performance industrial adhesives comprising reactive, light cure, two-part liquids, polyurethane, silicone, film, and fast cure products to the durable assembly, performance wood and textile, transportation, electronics, clean energy, aerospace and defense, appliance, heavy machinery, and insulating glass markets. The Construction Adhesives segment provides products used for commercial roofing, heating, ventilation, and air conditioning and insulation applications, as well as caulks and sealants for the consumer market and professional trade. The company sells its products directly to customers, as well as through distributors and retailers in North America, Latin America, Europe, India, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. H.B. Fuller Company was founded in 1887 and is headquartered in Saint Paul, Minnesota.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 7K people. Revenue per employee of $489K ranks in the below the sector median among Basic Materials peers, with revenue growing 6%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $17K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $3K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: H. B. Fuller Company is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $2.7B market cap on $3.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 28%.

The business throws off $121M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.73× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Above-average short interest at 5.6% of float
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Trading near the bottom of its 52-week range — the market is offering a discount
Piotroski score 7/9 — financials improving across profitability, leverage and efficiency
Insiders are net buyers (86% buy ratio) — insiders sell for many reasons but buy for only one
Large open-market insider purchases (net $0.8M) — management putting its own capital behind the business
39 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 10% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.77x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 13% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 34% and a beta of 0.95, it moves roughly with the market.
About $31.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 64% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 13% below its DCF fair value of $56.79, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 43%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $40.41 to $79.43 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 32% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $66.29 on average, 34% above the price.
The price implies 3.5% annual cash-flow growth, 1pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.45).
It runs a 28% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.73x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.0% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.6x net debt to EBITDA ($107.2M of cash against $2.0B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.6x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.5% over 3 years, 4.5% over 5 years and 5.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -13.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (4.1% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 7, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 3.7% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 6 purchases and 1 sale over the past year, net $786K bought.
It returns 4.2% a year to shareholders (2.3% in buybacks and 2.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 8.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 7,100 employees, each generates about $489K of revenue, 0.8x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 6.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $17K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.8M (6x revenue per employee).
